title: Check Your Tool’s Math
intro: In a 32-person ranking survey, Microsoft Forms named a winner the raw data didn't support.

learn.title: The undocumented weighting
learn.text:
Forms applied **positional weighting** that was never explained in the interface. It rewarded options that often landed near the top on average — not the option most people actually preferred.

The raw data showed a different option with far more first-place votes and most head-to-head wins.

try.q: What did the tool's method reward?
options: Appearing in the top three most often
try.explain: Which is a legitimate method — but not the one the team thought they were using.

learn.title: What he did instead
learn.text:
He exported the responses and rebuilt the rankings himself, comparing methods:

• **Pairwise wins with a Borda tie-breaker** — chosen, because it's easy to explain
• **The Schulze method** — handles preference cycles, but harder to reproduce

LLMs were useful for surfacing candidate methods.

Because the deadline forced a small sample, he had agreed beforehand how the results would be presented.

try.q: Why did he pick pairwise wins with a Borda tie-break over Schulze?
try.explain: Reproducibility and explainability beat sophistication here.

learn.title: The general lesson
learn.text:
Different aggregation methods **legitimately crown different winners**. That isn't a bug — it's why the method has to match the question.

So: find out what your tool does, say which method you used, and show the distribution rather than only the winner.

try.q: Two valid methods pick different winners. What does that mean?
options: The method must match the question
One of the methods is wrong
The ranking question was badly written
try.explain: Aggregation is a choice, and it should be a deliberate one.

test.q: How many people were in the ranking survey?
test.explain: Small enough that the presentation approach was agreed in advance.

test.q: What was wrong with the tool's behaviour?
test.explain: The weighting was legitimate but invisible.

test.q: What should you report alongside a ranking winner?
test.explain: Plus first-place votes and the method used.

test.q: What were LLMs useful for here?
test.explain: He still chose and verified the method himself.

test.q: What is the broader risk this illustrates?
options: Trusting a tool's summary without knowing its maths
test.explain: The tool was not broken; the assumption about it was.
